subject: Maths
central_question: How do factors, multiples, prime numbers, and divisibility patterns help us analyse whole numbers?
in_scope_units: 5.1 Common Multiples and Common Factors — repeated jumps, idli-vada, and shared factors
5.2 Prime Numbers — prime, composite, 1, and the Sieve of Eratosthenes
5.3 Co-prime Numbers — pairs sharing no factor other than 1 and co-prime art
5.4 Prime Factorisation — unique prime decomposition, products, co-prime checking, and divisibility
5.6 Fun with Numbers — special properties and prime-product puzzles
banned_topics: Formal proof of unique prime factorisation

known_pitfalls.correction: It has one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

known_pitfalls.claim: One partial factorisation can prove two numbers are co-prime.
known_pitfalls.correction: A missed factor may be common; use complete prime factorisations.

known_pitfalls.claim: Matching prime names is enough for divisibility.
known_pitfalls.correction: The number of occurrences of each prime factor also matters.

recommended_example_progression: Use idli-vada to identify multiples and common multiples.
Use jump sizes for factors and common factors.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes for primes up to 100.
Use 56 and 63 to expose incomplete-factor reasoning.
Apply prime factorisation and tests for 10, 5, 2, 4, and 8.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Use the Figure it Out and Math Talk exercises across Sections 5.1–5.6, ending with the special-number and prime-grid puzzles.
